name: Physarum

lumenary.blurb: Thousands of slime mould cells follow the scent trails of the others. They lay down a living transport network, drawn toward the light of your picture.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with bright shapes on dark ground

why: A slime mould is a single cell with no brain, and yet it finds short routes through a maze and builds networks that look like rail maps. Each part follows a simple rule: move toward the strongest scent of its own kind, and leave scent behind. Trails that many cells use grow stronger and trails nobody uses fade, so the best routes win.
how: Give each agent a position and heading, and let it sense the trail map at three points a distance d ahead: straight and 28 degrees left and right.
If the middle reading is highest, go straight; if both sides are higher, turn at random; otherwise turn toward the higher side.
Step one cell forward and deposit 0.3 units of chemical.
Each frame blur the trail map with a small kernel and multiply by the decay factor, so trails spread and fade.
Add food from the picture, so cells are drawn toward the light (or the dark) parts of it.
history: Toshiyuki Nakagaki and colleagues showed in 2000 that Physarum polycephalum can solve a maze. In 2010 Atsushi Tero and colleagues placed oat flakes in the pattern of cities around Tokyo and the mould grew a network similar to the real rail system. Jeff Jones published the agent model in 2010, and it has been used in generative art and network design research.
terms: A single celled organism that moves and feeds in a network.
A small program with its own position and rules.
Coordination through marks left in the environment.
paragraphs: The slime mould Physarum polycephalum has no brain, and yet it finds short routes between food sources and builds networks that resemble railway maps. Jeff Jones (2010) modelled it with agents that follow one another’s scent. Each agent has a position and a heading. It senses the trail map at three points a distance d ahead: straight on, and 28 degrees to the left and to the right. If the middle reading is the highest it goes straight on. If both sides are higher than the middle it turns at random one way or the other by the turning angle. If one side is higher it turns toward that side. Then it steps one cell forward and deposits 0.3 units of chemical there.

The trail map is a field in its own right. After every step it is blurred with the kernel (1 1 1 / 1 4 1 / 1 1 1) divided by 12, which spreads the scent a little, and multiplied by a decay factor, so old trails fade. What the agents sense is the trail plus 0.7 × the attraction slider × a food map, and the food map is the picture’s tone stretched to the full range (light or dark, your choice). The picture is the landscape of nutrients, and the mould builds its channels toward it. Two steps are made per frame, the agents are as many as a share of the grid cells, and pressing and dragging drops a burst of chemical, which agents follow.

equations.note: The left and right sensor readings (and the centre one with β = 0); T is the trail, F the food map and κ = 0.7 × the attraction slider.
The steering rule; τ is the sharpness of turns.
Diffusion and decay of the trail map after each step; δ is the trail-length slider.

presets.text: Long-lasting trails make thick, stable networks.
Strong attraction pulls the mould into the shape of your picture.
Seeking the dark grows around the bright shapes.
